extracted.intended_audience: students, translators, and readers interested in prose style, literary criticism, and translation practice
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative guidance for writing and translating literary prose, emphasizing punctuation, sentence-periods, economy, clarity, and fidelity in translation so that a version reads as an original.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punctuation as a tool of meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: The more accurate scholars of the last Age used punctuation (colons, semicolons, commas) to indicate finer meaning, emphasis, elision, and clause relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish leading clauses with colons and minor clauses with semicolons; use commas to mark emphasis, introduce relative clauses, indicate elision, or bring out the value of a phrase or epithet. Avoid treating the comma merely as a loop/bracket; do not substitute dashes and slovenly punctuation for precise marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overuse of full stops and jolting fragments
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern writing often favors many short sentences and jolting fragments, producing an untidy, noisy style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer longer, musical flowing periods where appropriate; avoid an excess of two-word sentences and disconnected fragments. Resist manuals that recommend chopping prose into constant short sentences — this sacrifices balance and can be a mark of haste rather than strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance and proportion in sentence and paragraph form
rubrics_metrics.description: Good prose assembles words, arranges sentences, and marshals them into careful periods with a sense of balance and proportion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write with structural harmony: vary sentence length but maintain an overall measured arrangement. Do not sacrifice form for speed; the old ordered periods achieve clarity without loss of vigour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and freedom from affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers of the best eighteenth-century style are prized for their exquisitely clear style, admirable common-sense, and freedom from tricks of affectation — 'simplex munditiis.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor unaffected prose that is plain in its neatness; avoid mannered ornament or artificial cleverness that draws attention away from sense. Simplicity aids discrimination and lucidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restraint and discriminating judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should be restrained in utterance so they may be discriminating in judgment: emphatic without noise, deep without obscurity, ornamental but not vulgar, carefully arranged but not stiff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate measured expression; make strong points without exaggeration or rhetorical noise. Strive for judgements that are precise and proportionate to evidence, avoiding superlatives and vague similes that 'deafen and perplex' the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and density of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Tacitus (as praised) exhibits 'redundancy of images, and a frugality of words' — many close images but few pointed words; 'put into his book as much as it will hold.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek concision: compress thought without impoverishing it. Favor precise, potent wording over diffuse exposition. Avoid diffuseness and needless verbosity; make every word earn its place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaningful diction and stylistic fitness
rubrics_metrics.description: Words and phrases should be admirably adapted to matter and conceptions; 'stile is a part of genius.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose diction that fits the subject and tone; avoid sonorous sentences whose sound outlives their meaning. Aim for language that makes a sudden and wonderful impression on the mind by fitting form to thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substance over rhetorical sound
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern readers are often 'ravished with a sonorous sentence' whose meaning does not long remain; this is a fault.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not prioritize ornate or sonorous phrasing at the expense of lasting sense. Evaluate prose by whether its meaning endures, not merely by its momentary rhetorical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation ought to read like an original
rubrics_metrics.description: A translation should 'read like an original'; good translators grasp the broad meaning and spirit of the author rather than producing correct but 'miserable English.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to convey spirit, tone, and literary effect, not merely literal correctness. Avoid renderings that are accurate in fact but poor as literature ('not the fire of Tacitus, but his embers'). Strive for English that stands as literature in its own right while faithful to the original's force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overlearned, lifeless translations
rubrics_metrics.description: Translations that are mere displays of learning frequently result in 'miserable English' — correct but not literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize readable, lively English; be wary of letting scholarship (e.g., slavish word-for-word rendering or over-noting) choke stylistic energy. Good translation balances fidelity with idiomatic, literary expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use classical reading as discipline against modern faults
rubrics_metrics.description: Converse with ancient authors (e.g., Latin practice) to counteract faults of diffuseness, obscurity, and excess common among modern writers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular study and practice in classical concise style can steady judgment and improve clarity and economy in modern prose. Techniques such as translating into Latin (Cardinal Newman's habit) are offered as disciplinary exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial fidelity to period punctuation and orthography when reproducing editions
rubrics_metrics.description: When reproducing older editions, observe original punctuation and orthography where possible to preserve the dignity of the original page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modernize cautiously; respect historical punctuation patterns (colons, semicolons, capitalization) that contribute to period rhythm and meaning. Avoid wholesale modernization that erases useful features of the original style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplementary editorial apparatus aids comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: Maps, genealogical tables, and judicious notes (as in Church & Brodribb's translation) are of the greatest service and sometimes amusing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When preparing editions or translations, include helpful apparatus (maps, tables, explanatory notes) to orient readers and enhance usefulness; but keep notes balanced so they do not overwhelm the literary text.
